why_angle: The cited guides give only maker specs. The small-format guide says outright 'All numbers are manufacturer specs', and neither cited page reports a measured deviation for any scanner. This page has HafenCity University Hamburg's 2026 test against a ZEISS ATOS 5 reference on a 3D-printed PLA part. It also has Notebookcheck's 150 mm gauge-block result for the Ferret Pro and 3D Printing Industry's reference-block test of the Seal. Those results move the pick from ChatGPT's POP 3 Plus, the noisiest scanner in the lab test, to the 3DMakerpro Moose.

page.title: Best 3D Scanner for 3D Printing (2026): Tested Picks by Part Type
page.desc: Which 3D scanner for 3D printing came closest to the real part? Lab and reviewer measurements for the 3DMakerpro Moose and Seal, Revopoint MetroX and POP 3 Plus, and Creality Ferret Pro, with today's prices.
page.answer: Short answer. The best 3D scanner for 3D printing is the 3DMakerpro Moose ($419): in HafenCity University Hamburg's 2026 test of a 3D-printed part, its scan deviated 0.10 mm (standard deviation) from the reference, against 0.66 mm for the Revopoint POP 3 Plus.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Moose vs POP 3 Plus on the same printed part: 0.66 mm ÷ 0.10 mm = 6.6 times the scatter. The worst outliers spread 14.08 mm on the POP 3 Plus and 1.36 mm on the Moose.
  • Moose vs MetroX on the printed part: both have a 0.10 mm standard deviation. The MetroX's stray points spread 8.04 mm against the Moose's 1.36 mm, and 8.04 ÷ 1.36 = 5.9 times as much stray material to clean off before printing.
  • Moose vs MetroX on a flat plate: 0.60 mm ÷ 0.29 mm = 2.1, so the Moose scattered about twice as much on a featureless flat surface.
  • Ferret Pro on Notebookcheck's gauge block: 0.335 mm ÷ 150 mm = 0.22 % of the part's length.
  • Seal on 3D Printing Industry's block: 0.16 mm ÷ 0.02 mm = 8 times larger on one axis than on the other two.
  • Price: the Moose and Seal both list at $419. The MetroX Standard Edition is $999 − $419 = $580 more and was sold out at Revopoint on 2026-11-17.

What the scanners measured against a reference

Kersten, Marsmann and Przybilla at HafenCity University Hamburg scanned five objects with the handheld scanners and compared every scan with a ZEISS ATOS 5 reference. One object was a 100 × 100 × 100 mm staircase with five 20 mm steps, printed in PLA on a Prusa, which is the kind of part a shopper scans to reprint. The Moose was used in handheld EasyScan mode. The Revopoint scanners were used in turntable mode with markers placed nearby. The paper's conclusion: the Moose "proved to be the most accurate system" among the low-cost scanners.

On the bust and the porous figure, the Moose matched the high-end MARVELSCAN. Its weak spot is flat, featureless surfaces. {buy:3dmakerpro-moose-3d-scanner}

Notebookcheck's Silvio Werner scanned a 150 mm gauge block, which a calibrated caliper read at 150.005 mm, with the Ferret Pro. CrealityScan measured it at 149.67 mm. Werner adds that this one result does not show Creality's 0.1 mm specification is overstated, because the error also depends on which points you pick to measure between.

In 3D Printing Industry's review, Alex Tyrer-Jones scanned a 15 × 20 × 25 mm block with the Seal in turntable mode. The scan came within 0.02 mm on two axes and was off by −0.16 mm on the third. A sprayed motorcycle indicator measured −0.053 mm off and a sprayed e-scooter suspension part 0.104 mm off. That test dates from February 2024. {buy:3dmakerpro-seal-3d-scanner}

Not recommended

Revopoint POP 3 Plus, for parts that have to fit. Of the scanners tested at HafenCity University Hamburg, it scattered the most on the printed part, the bust, the porous figure and the granite plate: 0.66 mm on the printed part and 1.26 mm on the bust. At $526 it costs $107 more than the Moose, which scattered 0.10 mm on the same part. It still makes sense if you want color scans and the printed copy doesn't need to fit anything.
